mcqs.q: Complications of exodontia are categorized into which two groups?
opts: Operative and postoperative
Local and systemic
Hard tissue and soft tissue
Immediate and delayed
mcqs.explain: The division is by timing relative to the extraction itself, not by tissue type or by anatomical extent.

mcqs.q: The commonest complication associated with forceps extraction is:
opts: Fracture of the tooth
Fracture of the alveolar bone
Dislocation of the mandible
Oroantral communication
mcqs.explain: Alveolar fracture is also common, but tooth fracture heads the list of operative complications.

mcqs.q: Non-vital teeth are prone to fracture during extraction because they are:
opts: Brittle or badly decayed
Firmly ankylosed to the bone
Surrounded by denser alveolar bone
More mobile than vital teeth
mcqs.explain: Loss of vitality leaves the dentine dehydrated and unsupported, and such teeth are often heavily destroyed by caries as well.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a MECHANICAL obstruction that may make complete removal with forceps impossible?
opts: Severe curvature of the roots or hypercementosis
An amalgam restoration in the crown
A periapical radiolucency
Mobility of the adjacent tooth
mcqs.explain: Both features physically lock the root within the socket so that the tooth cannot follow a simple path of withdrawal.

mcqs.q: Closing the beaks of the forceps too tightly on the tooth causes fracture by:
opts: Applying a crushing force to the crown
Preventing the blood supply reaching the periodontal ligament
Expanding the socket prematurely
Forcing the tooth into the sinus
mcqs.explain: The beaks must grip the root, not crush the crown — and the adjustment must be completed before any movement begins.

mcqs.q: Attempting the extraction movement BEFORE completing the adjustment of the forceps to the tooth results in:
opts: Fracture of the tooth
Dislocation of the mandible
Injury to the inferior alveolar nerve
Fracture of the tuberosity
mcqs.explain: Until the beaks are fully seated on the root the force is concentrated on the crown, which then shears off.

mcqs.q: After the tooth fractures during extraction, the operator may:
opts: Grasp the remaining roots and extract them, or use the surgical technique to remove them
Leave the roots in situ and review in six months
Immediately refer all cases to a maxillofacial surgeon
Section the adjacent tooth to gain access
mcqs.explain: Either a renewed forceps or elevator application, or an open surgical approach, is appropriate depending on access.

mcqs.q: Why is it advisable to warn the patient beforehand that a tooth may fracture during extraction?
opts: So that when it happens the patient will not lose confidence
Because the law requires a written warning for every extraction
To justify charging an additional surgical fee
Because the patient can then choose a different anaesthetic
mcqs.explain: This applies when examination shows that fracture may accidentally take place or be purposely caused.

mcqs.q: Fracture of part of the alveolar process is especially common in difficult extractions involving:
opts: Widely divergent, hypercementosed or ankylosed roots
Mobile teeth with advanced periodontal disease
Teeth with large composite restorations
Recently erupted permanent teeth
mcqs.explain: Mobile periodontally involved teeth are the easy ones; it is the mechanically locked roots that take the bone with them.

mcqs.q: The MOST likely site for alveolar bone fracture is the:
opts: Buccal cortical plate of the maxillary canine and maxillary molars
Lingual plate of the mandibular incisors
Palatal plate of the maxillary incisors
Buccal plate of the mandibular premolars
mcqs.explain: The upper first molar with widely divergent roots is specifically named as the highest-risk tooth.

mcqs.q: During forceps extraction, how can alveolar fracture best be prevented?
opts: If mobility does not respond to appropriate force, switch to the surgical technique
Apply steadily increasing force until the tooth moves
Use a wider forceps beak to spread the load
Complete the extraction under general anaesthesia
mcqs.explain: Converting to an open surgical extraction is the single rule that prevents most bony complications.

mcqs.q: A fractured piece of alveolar bone that REMAINS ATTACHED to the soft tissues should be:
opts: Replaced and left to heal
Removed and the edges smoothed
Removed and sent for histopathology
Splinted to the adjacent teeth for 6–8 weeks
mcqs.explain: Its soft tissue attachment preserves the blood supply, so the fragment remains viable.

mcqs.q: A piece of bone COMPLETELY DETACHED from the bone and overlying soft tissues should usually be:
opts: Removed, as it has lost its blood supply, and the sharp edges smoothed
Replaced and sutured into position
Left in the socket to act as a graft
Crushed and packed into the socket
mcqs.explain: A fragment with no blood supply will sequestrate, so it is removed at the time.

mcqs.q: Fracture of the maxillary tuberosity occurs most often during extraction of:
opts: A second or third maxillary molar
A maxillary canine
A mandibular third molar
A maxillary first premolar
mcqs.explain: The tuberosity lies immediately distal to these teeth and may be hollowed out by the sinus.

mcqs.q: Which of the following predisposes to tuberosity fracture?
opts: Weakening of the tuberosity by extension of the sinus into it
The presence of a large composite restoration
Previous orthodontic treatment
A shallow palatal vault
mcqs.explain: Ankylosis of the tooth and the use of a distal luxation movement are the other two named causes.

mcqs.q: If a tuberosity fracture occurs, the extraction should:
opts: NOT be continued — it destroys the tuberosity, lacerates tissue and causes a fistula
Be completed quickly, before further bone detaches
Be continued using a stronger pair of forceps
Be completed under general anaesthesia the same visit
mcqs.explain: Persisting converts a manageable fracture into a destroyed tuberosity with an antral opening.

mcqs.q: If a tuberosity fracture is noticed in proper time, the surgeon should:
opts: Stabilize the tooth and try to separate it from the bone surgically without further detachment
Remove the tooth and the entire mobile bone segment together
Pack the socket and review in one week
Reduce the fracture with intermaxillary fixation
mcqs.explain: Separating the tooth from the bone preserves the tuberosity, which is needed for later denture support.

mcqs.q: If the fractured tuberosity is mobile and cannot be dissected from the tooth, the best line of treatment may be to splint the tooth to the adjacent teeth for:
opts: 6–8 weeks
1–2 weeks
3–4 weeks
12–16 weeks
mcqs.explain: The fractured bone heals in that time, and the tooth can then be extracted surgically — but only if the extraction can be delayed.

mcqs.q: Fracture of the jaw during extraction occurs most often in the:
opts: Mandible
Maxilla
Zygomatic arch
Palatine bone
mcqs.explain: It results from excessive force used without adequate support, and the mandible is the unsupported mobile bone.

mcqs.q: Management of a jaw fractured during extraction is:
opts: Surgical, by fixation of the fractured jaw
Conservative, with a soft diet alone
Splinting of the adjacent teeth for 6–8 weeks
Immediate re-extraction of the remaining roots
mcqs.explain: The fracture must be reduced and fixed like any other mandibular fracture.

mcqs.q: In the panoramic radiograph showing a fractured mandibular angle after third molar luxation, the stated cause was that:
opts: Not enough surrounding bone had been removed to create an unimpeded pathway
The patient had an undiagnosed cyst
The local anaesthetic had not taken effect
The wrong forceps had been selected
mcqs.explain: Without bone removal the tooth cannot move, so the force is transmitted to the jaw itself.

mcqs.q: When an extensive pathological lesion surrounds an impacted tooth, the radiograph warns the surgeon that:
opts: The risk of jaw fracture during the surgical procedure is great
The tooth will be easier to remove because the bone is softer
The inferior alveolar nerve will certainly be transected
An oroantral communication is inevitable
mcqs.explain: The lesion has already weakened the bone, so normal operative forces may now fracture it.

mcqs.q: Gingival and mucosal laceration during extraction may result from:
opts: Improper application or slipping of the instrument, or alveolar fracture taking mucosa
Excessive local anaesthetic infiltration volume
Prolonged operating time on its own
Inadequate suction during the procedure
mcqs.explain: Both a direct instrument injury and an indirect bony avulsion can tear the covering mucosa.

mcqs.q: Management of a lacerated gingiva after extraction requires:
opts: Proper suturing of the lacerated gingiva
Excision of the torn margins and secondary healing
Electrocautery of the wound edges
A periodontal dressing for two weeks
mcqs.explain: Proper suturing is stated to be all that is required in this condition.

mcqs.q: Unintentional extraction of an ADJACENT tooth may occur because of:
opts: Operating rapidly and consequently misdirecting the forceps
Using an elevator rather than forceps
Extracting under local rather than general anaesthesia
Applying the forceps too slowly
mcqs.explain: Lack of vision from accumulated blood and saliva, and fusion of adjacent teeth, are the other two causes given.

mcqs.q: A loosened or avulsed adjacent tooth should be:
opts: Pushed back and splinted if necessary, then followed up for any complication
Extracted at the same visit
Left alone, as it will reattach spontaneously
Root treated immediately before repositioning
mcqs.explain: Repositioning, splinting and follow-up give the tooth the best chance of reattachment.

mcqs.q: Injury to the lip, tongue or cheek during extraction can be avoided by:
opts: Proper retraction using the fingers of the left hand during the extraction
Using a mouth prop on the opposite side
Operating only under general anaesthesia
Applying petroleum jelly to the lips before starting
mcqs.explain: The non-dominant hand both retracts the soft tissues and supports the jaw throughout.

mcqs.q: A burn of the lower lip during a surgical extraction is caused by:
opts: Overheating of a surgical handpiece (micromotor)
Prolonged contact with the local anaesthetic solution
The chemical action of the irrigating fluid
Electrosurgical current leakage
mcqs.explain: This is why the handpiece temperature must be checked and copious irrigation used.

mcqs.q: The two classic sites of soft tissue injury from elevator slippage are:
opts: The sublingual area and the posterior palate
The upper lip and the labial sulcus
The soft palate and the uvula
The buccal mucosa and the retromolar pad
mcqs.explain: An elevator that slips travels at speed and buries itself in whatever lies in its path.

mcqs.q: A root may be displaced into the submandibular space if:
opts: The lingual plate is very thin or has been perforated by previous infection
The buccal plate is unusually thick
The patient has a deep overbite
The tooth is ankylosed
mcqs.explain: The lingual plate is the floor-of-mouth side of the mandibular socket, and a defect there opens directly into the space.

mcqs.q: The FIRST attempt at retrieving a root displaced into the submandibular space is to:
opts: Apply pressure in the submandibular region and try to pick the root out through the socket
Make an immediate extraoral submandibular incision
Refer the patient for CT imaging before any intervention
Leave the root and prescribe antibiotics
mcqs.explain: If the root cannot be retrieved by this attempt, the surgical method becomes the method of choice.

mcqs.q: Dislocation of the mandible during extraction is usually the result of:
opts: Inadequate support to the mandible during the extraction
Excessive use of the elevator
Local anaesthetic injected into the joint capsule
Extraction of a maxillary third molar
mcqs.explain: The mandible must be supported by the operator's other hand against the downward extraction force.

mcqs.q: Which sign of mandibular dislocation is seen IN FRONT OF THE EAR?
opts: A visible depression
A visible swelling
Bruising of the overlying skin
An audible click on movement
mcqs.explain: The depression marks the empty glenoid fossa after the condyle has moved anteriorly.

mcqs.q: During reduction of a dislocated mandible, the operator stands:
opts: In front of the patient and applies downward and backward pressure on the molars
Behind the patient and applies upward pressure on the chin
To the patient's right and applies lateral pressure on the ramus
Behind the patient and applies downward pressure on the incisors
mcqs.explain: The thumbs are protected first, and the other fingers simultaneously elevate the chin.

mcqs.q: In an EDENTULOUS patient, where is the reduction pressure applied?
opts: On the alveolar ridge
On the mental region only
On the angle of the mandible
On the coronoid process
mcqs.explain: The ridge replaces the molar teeth as the point of downward and backward pressure.

mcqs.q: Injury to the inferior alveolar nerve during extraction is:
opts: Uncommon with erupted molars, but a risk where the canal nears the wisdom tooth apex
Equally likely with all of the mandibular teeth
Commonest during extraction of mandibular incisors
Impossible when local anaesthesia is fully adequate
mcqs.explain: Any blind use of the elevator or curette in the third molar socket should be avoided for this reason.

mcqs.q: Oroantral communication occurs most often during extraction of the:
opts: Maxillary molars
Maxillary premolars
Maxillary canines
Mandibular molars
mcqs.explain: The premolars are affected to a lesser extent; the molars sit directly beneath the antral floor.

mcqs.q: The root MOST frequently displaced into the maxillary sinus is the:
opts: Palatal root of the maxillary first molar
Mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar
Distobuccal root of the maxillary second molar
Single root of the maxillary second premolar
mcqs.explain: Its apex lies closest to the antral floor and it is the hardest root to control during elevation.

mcqs.q: Apical infections and other pathological processes favour sinus perforation because:
opts: The bone between root and sinus may already be destroyed by the pathological process
They make the affected root considerably more brittle
They cause the sinus to contract away from the roots
They markedly thicken the sinus lining membrane
mcqs.explain: The protective bony plate has already been resorbed before the extraction begins.

mcqs.q: Which clinical sign suggests that a sinus perforation has occurred?
opts: The patient finds some blood or water coming from the nose
The patient reports numbness of the lower lip
The socket bleeds more than usual
The patient cannot close the mouth
mcqs.explain: Disappearance of the root from the socket is the other classic sign, and the nose-blowing test can confirm the opening.

mcqs.q: The main sequelae that must be prevented after a sinus perforation are:
opts: Maxillary sinusitis and formation of a chronic oroantral fistula
Osteomyelitis and trismus
Dry socket and secondary haemorrhage
Nerve paraesthesia and facial swelling
mcqs.explain: Both arise from persistent communication between the contaminated oral cavity and the antrum.

mcqs.q: If a root or a tooth has been forced into the sinus, it should be:
opts: Removed surgically in most cases BEFORE closing the fistula
Left in place and the fistula closed over it
Removed only if the patient develops sinusitis
Pushed further into the antrum and left
mcqs.explain: A foreign body left in the antrum will maintain infection no matter how well the fistula is closed.

mcqs.q: The Caldwell–Luc surgical technique is used to:
opts: Remove a root from the maxillary sinus
Close an oroantral fistula with a buccal advancement flap
Reduce a fractured tuberosity
Retrieve a root from the submandibular space
mcqs.explain: Access is gained through the canine fossa above the buccal sulcus.

mcqs.q: An oroantral communication of 2 mm or less requires:
opts: Ensure a good blood clot and give strict clot-protection instructions — nothing more
Suturing of the socket to maintain the blood clot
Referral to a surgeon for a flap closure
Immediate Caldwell–Luc exploration of the sinus
mcqs.explain: Suturing is added for 2–6 mm; a flap is needed above 6 mm.

mcqs.q: An oroantral communication of 2–6 mm is managed by:
opts: Suturing the socket to maintain the blood clot, plus the usual clot precautions
Clot precautions alone, with no suturing
Referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for flap closure
Packing with ribbon gauze for one week
mcqs.explain: This is the middle band of the size-based protocol.

mcqs.q: An oroantral fistula larger than 6 mm requires:
opts: Referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon, as closure will need a certain type of flap
Suturing of the socket alone
Clot precautions and antibiotics only
Extraction of the adjacent tooth to allow closure
mcqs.explain: A defect of this size will not close over a clot and needs a designed soft tissue flap.

mcqs.q: Which instruction is given to protect the clot over an oroantral communication?
opts: Avoid blowing the nose, sucking on straws, violent sneezing and smoking
Rinse vigorously with hot salt water every hour
Chew on the affected side to maintain circulation
Sleep flat without a pillow for 48 hours
mcqs.explain: Every one of these raises or lowers pressure across the opening and would dislodge the clot.

mcqs.q: In addition to clot protection, which medications may be prescribed after a sinus perforation?
opts: Antibiotics and a nasal decongestant
Corticosteroids and an antihistamine
An antifungal and a mouthwash
An anticoagulant and an analgesic
mcqs.explain: The decongestant keeps the ostium patent so the antrum can drain normally while the clot organises.

mcqs.q: To PREVENT sinus perforation, a preoperative radiograph showing possible sinus floor involvement should lead the surgeon to:
opts: Avoid closed forceps extraction — do a surgical extraction with sectioning
Use a wider forceps to distribute the applied force
Extract more rapidly to minimise the contact time
Postpone the extraction indefinitely
mcqs.explain: Sectioning removes the tooth in pieces, so no single force acts on the antral floor.

mcqs.q: If a tooth is SWALLOWED during extraction:
opts: It will pass through the alimentary canal
Emergency bronchoscopy is required
It must be retrieved endoscopically within 24 hours
The patient should be given an emetic
mcqs.explain: Aspiration, by contrast, is a genuine emergency that must be managed quickly.

mcqs.q: A tooth passing beyond the pharynx is described as occurring due to:
opts: Neglect and carelessness on the part of the operator
An unavoidable anatomical variation
Inadequate local anaesthesia
Excessive force during luxation
mcqs.explain: It is very rare, and prevented by throat protection and a secure grip on the tooth at all times.

mcqs.q: The single factor running through almost every operative complication of exodontia is:
opts: Excessive, uncontrolled force
Inadequate local anaesthesia
Poor patient selection
Insufficient operating time
mcqs.explain: Tooth fracture, alveolar and tuberosity fracture, jaw fracture, soft tissue laceration and TMJ dislocation all trace back to it.

saqs.q: List the operative complications of exodontia.
saqs.a: Fracture of the tooth · alveolar bone · the jaw · the tuberosity · gingival or mucosal laceration · loosening or extraction of an adjacent tooth · injury to lip, cheek or tongue · disturbing a restoration or prosthesis · dislocation of the mandible · displacement of a root into the submandibular space · maxillary sinus involvement · inferior alveolar nerve injury · tooth passed beyond the pharynx · extraction of or injury to an unerupted tooth.

list: Fracture of the tooth
Fracture of the alveolar bone
Fracture of the jaw
Fracture of the tuberosity
Gingival and/or mucosal laceration
Loosening or extraction of an adjacent tooth
Injury to the lip, cheek or tongue
Disturbing a restoration or prosthesis
Dislocation of the mandible
Displacement of a root into the submandibular space
Maxillary sinus involvement
Injury to the inferior alveolar nerve
Tooth passed beyond the pharynx
Extraction of, or injury to, an unerupted tooth

saqs.q: Give the causes of tooth fracture during forceps extraction.
saqs.a: Non-vital, brittle or badly decayed teeth · mechanical obstruction (severe root curvature, hypercementosis) · improper selection or application of the instrument · improper technique · patient interference · abnormal supporting structures · closing the beaks too tightly · starting the movement before the forceps is fully adjusted · lack of control of the instrument.

list: Non-vital teeth — brittle or badly decayed
Mechanical obstruction — severe root curvature or hypercementosis making complete forceps removal impossible
Improper selection or application of the instrument
Improper extraction technique
Interference by the patient
Abnormality of the supporting structures
Closing the beaks too tightly, with crushing force
Attempting the movement before the forceps is fully adjusted to the tooth
Lack of control of the instrument throughout

saqs.q: Describe the management of a fractured alveolar plate, distinguishing attached from detached fragments.
saqs.a: ATTACHED to soft tissue — retains its blood supply; replace it and let it heal. COMPLETELY DETACHED — has lost its blood supply; remove it and smooth the sharp edges. PREVENTION — if mobility does not respond to an appropriate force, do not apply more; convert to the surgical technique.

head: Fragment
Management
rows: REMAINS ATTACHED to the soft tissues
retains its blood supply — replace it and leave it to heal
COMPLETELY DETACHED from bone and overlying soft tissue
has lost its blood supply — usually remove it, and smooth the sharp edges

ans.text: Prevention — if tooth mobility does not respond to an appropriate amount of force, do not apply more; convert to the surgical technique.

saqs.q: Why does fracture of the maxillary tuberosity occur, and what must the operator NOT do when it happens?
saqs.a: It occurs on extracting a second or third molar, especially if the tooth is ankylosed, the tuberosity is weakened by sinus extension, or a distal luxation movement is used. The operator finds himself grasping a large detached bone segment with the tooth still seated in it. The extraction must NOT be continued — it destroys the tuberosity, lacerates soft tissue and often causes an oroantral fistula.

list: Extraction of a second or third molar is attempted
The tooth is ankylosed to the bone
The tuberosity is weakened by extension of the sinus into it
A distal movement is used for luxation of the molar

ans.text: The operator finds himself grasping a large segment of detached bone with the tooth still firmly seated in the broken, moving part.
The extraction must NOT be continued — it will result in a destroyed tuberosity, lacerated soft tissues and often an oroantral fistula.

saqs.q: Outline the stepwise management of a fractured maxillary tuberosity.
saqs.a: 1 Stop the extraction. 2 If noticed in time, stabilize the tooth and separate it surgically without further detaching bone. 3 If the tuberosity is mobile and cannot be dissected free, splint the tooth to the adjacent teeth for 6–8 weeks and extract surgically then — only if the extraction can be delayed. 4 Otherwise smooth the sharp edges and manage the lacerated soft tissue. 5 Check for and manage any oroantral communication.

steps: If noticed in proper time, stabilize the tooth and try to separate it from the bone surgically, without further detachment

If the tuberosity is mobile and cannot be dissected from the tooth, splint the tooth to the adjacent teeth for 6–8 weeks so the bone heals, then extract surgically — logical only if the extraction can be delayed
If these fail or cannot be used, smooth the sharp edges of the remaining bone and manage the lacerated soft tissues
Check for and manage any oroantral communication

saqs.q: How does an adjacent tooth come to be loosened or unintentionally extracted, and how is it managed?
saqs.a: LOOSENING — usually improper application of forceps or elevator; avoidable with sufficient care. UNINTENTIONAL EXTRACTION — operating too fast and misdirecting the forceps, poor vision from accumulated blood and saliva, or fused adjacent teeth. MANAGEMENT — push the tooth back, splint if necessary, and follow up.

head: Event
Cause
rows: LOOSENING
improper application of the forceps or elevator — avoidable with sufficient care
UNINTENTIONAL EXTRACTION
operating too rapidly and misdirecting the forceps · lack of vision when blood and saliva accumulate · adjacent teeth fused together

ans.text: Management — the loosened or avulsed tooth should be pushed back and splinted if necessary, then followed up for any complication.

saqs.q: Describe the clinical presentation of mandibular dislocation during extraction and the technique of reduction.
saqs.a: PRESENTATION — usually from inadequate support of the mandible. The patient suddenly cannot close the mouth, with TMJ pain and a visible depression in front of the ear; unilateral or bilateral. REDUCTION — stand in front, protect the thumbs, apply downward and backward pressure on the molars (or the ridge if edentulous) while the other fingers elevate the chin.

rows: PRESENTATION

usually the result of inadequate support of the mandible. Suddenly the patient cannot close the mouth, with pain in and around the TMJ and a visible depression in front of the ear. May be unilateral or bilateral
REDUCTION

the operator stands in front of the patient and, after protecting the thumbs, applies downward and backward pressure on the molar teeth — or the alveolar ridge if edentulous — while the other fingers at the chin elevate it, relocating the condyle

saqs.q: Explain why oroantral communication occurs, and name the root most often displaced into the sinus.
saqs.a: It occurs on extracting maxillary molars, less often premolars, especially if the sinus is pneumatized into the alveolus, the apex is very near the sinus, or the apex perforates the floor. Apical infection and other pathology favour perforation, as the bone between root and sinus may already be destroyed. The root most often displaced is the PALATAL ROOT OF THE MAXILLARY FIRST MOLAR.

list: The sinus is pneumatized into the alveolus
The root apex is very near the sinus
The apex perforates the floor of the sinus
Apical infection and other pathology — the bone between root and sinus may already have been completely destroyed

ans.text: It occurs during extraction of the maxillary molars, or to a lesser extent the premolars. The root most frequently displaced into the sinus is the PALATAL ROOT OF THE MAXILLARY FIRST MOLAR.

saqs.q: How is an oroantral communication diagnosed?
saqs.a: Blood or water from the nose · the root has disappeared from the socket · a periapical curette enters deeper than normal, as far as the angle of its first curvature · the nose-blowing test · confirmation on a good X-ray.

list: The patient finds blood or water coming from the nose
If a root was displaced, it has disappeared from the socket
A periapical curette enters the alveolus deeper than normal — as far as the angle of its first curvature
The nose-blowing test can confirm the fistula
Confirmation by a good X-ray examination

saqs.q: Give the size-based protocol for closure of an oroantral fistula.
saqs.a: SMALL (≤2 mm) — nothing extra; ensure a good blood clot and give strict instructions (no nose-blowing, straws, violent sneezing or smoking); antibiotics and a nasal decongestant may be prescribed. MEDIUM (2–6 mm) — suture the socket to maintain the clot, with the same precautions. LARGE (>6 mm) — refer to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon; closure needs a flap.

head: Size
Management
rows: SMALL — 2 mm or less

no additional measures; ensure a good blood clot and give strict instructions to avoid disturbing it — no nose-blowing, straws, violent sneezing or smoking. Antibiotics and a nasal decongestant may be prescribed
MEDIUM — 2–6 mm
suturing of the socket to maintain the blood clot, plus the same clot-protection precautions
LARGE — >6 mm
refer to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — closure will need a flap

saqs.a: Prevention is better than management. A preoperative X-ray evaluates the relation of the tooth to the sinus. If sinus floor fracture is possible, avoid a closed forceps extraction and do a surgical extraction with tooth sectioning and the least, controlled force.

ans.text: As with all complications, prevention is better than management. A preoperative X-ray should evaluate the relation of the tooth to the sinus. If there is a possibility of sinus floor fracture, avoid a closed forceps extraction and perform a surgical extraction with tooth sectioning, using the least, controlled amount of force.

saqs.q: What is the risk to the inferior alveolar nerve during extraction, and how is it minimised?
saqs.a: Injury is very uncommon with erupted molars. But with the lower wisdom tooth the canal may lie close to the apex, so any blind use of the elevator or curette must be avoided, as it may traumatise the nerve.

ans.text: Injury is very uncommon during extraction of the erupted molar teeth. However, with the lower wisdom tooth the canal may be close to the apex, so any blind use of the elevator or curette should be avoided — it may traumatise the nerve.

saqs.q: Distinguish between a swallowed and an aspirated tooth.
saqs.a: Very rare, and due to neglect and carelessness. A SWALLOWED tooth passes through the alimentary canal. An ASPIRATED tooth is an EMERGENCY and must be managed quickly.

ans.text: Very rare — its occurrence is due to neglect and carelessness on the part of the operator.

head: SWALLOWED
ASPIRATED
rows: passes through the alimentary canal
an EMERGENCY — must be managed quickly
